name: Ironside Thermal Workwear Henley
description:
Ironside makes gear for people who work outdoors in the Great Lakes corridor, and the Thermal Henley is the backbone of their catalog — a three-button placket henley in a mid-weight brushed synth-cotton that holds heat in wet conditions without becoming a sauna when you're moving. The cuffs are slightly extended to tuck under gloves without bunching, and the collar is designed to sit flat under a high-vis vest or stand alone on a mild day. Colors run to dark slate, rust, and a deep pine green that Ironside has been printing since the brand launched in 2171.

This is a shirt for dock workers, construction crews, municipal maintenance techs, and anyone who needs to be outside when the lake wind comes in cold and sharp off the water. It washes hard and holds its shape. The stitching at the shoulder seams is reinforced with a secondary bar-tack, and the fabric has been pre-shrunk to within a centimeter of its life. Nothing fancy. Does what it says.
materials: reinforced bar-tack stitching at stress points
what_it_says: You work with your hands and you've learned what clothing is actually worth buying.
story_hooks: A specific run of Ironside Thermal Henleys from 2198 was accidentally woven with a conductive thread variant — they faintly register on proximity sensors, a fact that someone in logistics has been quietly exploiting.
An Ironside in rust-orange is the unofficial color of a particular Tier 2 labor union chapter — wearing it to a management meeting sends a message.
A worker found the shirt still warm on a job site where the previous occupant vanished mid-shift.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian henley with a masculine, no-nonsense silhouette. The garment reads as sturdy and functional—the kind of shirt that looks equally at home under a high-vis vest or worn alone on a cool dock. The slightly extended cuffs and flat collar give it a deliberately practical cut that prioritizes layering and real-world wear over fashion.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through the torso with subtle taper at the waist. Sleeves are straight-cut and slightly roomy to accommodate movement and glove-tucking. The length hits mid-hip, designed to stay tucked or worn loose depending on the job.
physical_description.primary_material: Mid-weight brushed synth-cotton blend—a durable engineered fabric that balances thermal retention with breathability. Pre-shrunk to minimize future size changes.
physical_description.texture: Brushed surface with a soft nap that traps warmth. The weave is tight and honest, showing no attempt to hide its industrial construction. Faint texture from the brush finish gives it visual depth without being ornamental.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary options: dark slate (neutral gray-blue), rust (oxidized orange-brown), and deep pine green. All are muted, practical palette choices that hide work stains and complement industrial environments.
physical_description.closures: Three-button placket henley closure in dark matte hardware. Buttons are functional and oversized enough to operate with gloved hands.
distinctive_features: Extended cuffs designed to tuck under gloves without bunching
Reinforced shoulder seams with visible secondary bar-tack stitching
Flat collar engineered to wear under high-vis vests or standalone
Intentional lack of branding—only subtle woven label at side seam
Fabric pre-shrunk to minimize size drift after washing
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 functional. This is working-class infrastructure—not cheap, but not luxury. Built for people who earn their living outdoors.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by dock workers, construction crews, municipal maintenance technicians, and anyone in the Great Lakes corridor who works in cold, wet conditions. The shirt signals competence, durability, and indifference to fashion trends. It says 'I have a job to do and this gets the job done.'
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in but well-maintained. Fading at collar and cuffs from repeated washing. Possible fabric pilling at high-friction areas (upper arms, under arms). May show faint stains that have survived multiple wash cycles. The garment improves with wear—never looks deliberately distressed, but gains character through genuine use.
